bib.title: Survival Analysis and the EM Algorithm (Chapter 9 of Computer Age Statistical Inference)

question: How can survival times that are censored (known only to exceed a value) be summarised, compared between groups and regressed on covariates, and how does the same missing-data logic lead to the EM algorithm?
contributions: Develops life tables, the Kaplan-Meier estimate, the log-rank test and Cox proportional hazards as a progression of increasingly computational and increasingly conditional (Fisherian) inference.
Presents the EM algorithm via the fake-data principle and shows Kaplan-Meier is self-consistent.

results.claim: A life table estimates a 30-year-old's chance of surviving past 80 as 0.506 from one year of data, by multiplying (1 - hazard) across ages.
results.setup: Table 9.1, fictitious insurance company, deaths based on true 2010 US male rates; hazard h_i = y_i/n_i per age, S = product of (1 - h_k) from age 30; assumes hazards do not change over time.
results.quote: estimated to be 0.506 in the table

results.claim: Arm B (chemotherapy plus radiation) has median survival 324 days against 182 days for Arm A (chemotherapy only), by Kaplan-Meier.
results.n: 51 in Arm A, 45 in Arm B
results.setup: NCOG head/neck cancer randomized trial, survival in days with censoring (more censoring in Arm B); per-timepoint 95% Greenwood intervals overlap enough to leave the comparison unclear.
results.quote: survival estimate occurs at 324 days, compared with 182 days for Arm A

results.claim: In month 6 of NCOG the expected Arm A deaths under equal hazards are 5.42 with hypergeometric variance 2.28, against 7 observed.
results.metric: E and V for one 2x2 table
results.setup: E = nA*nd/n, V = nA nB nd ns / (n^2 (n-1)), computed on the month-6 two-by-two table (y=7 Arm A deaths).
results.note: Text extraction renders = as D and . as colon.

results.claim: The log-rank test on the monthly-binned NCOG data gives Z = 2.27, one-sided p about 0.012, moderate evidence that Arm B is better.
results.setup: Sum of (y_i - E_i) over 47 months divided by sqrt(sum V_i); sum y_i = 42, sum E_i = 32.9, sum V_i = 16.0; Z ~ N(0,1) under equal hazards by CLT.
results.note: Text prints 'signiﬁcant at the one-sided 0.012 level'; the sums are printed as 42, 32.9, 16.0.

results.claim: Parametric (cubic-linear spline logistic) hazard estimates put Arm B hazard about 2.5 times lower than Arm A after the first year, with non-overlapping 95% limits at 15 and 30 months.
results.metric: hazard ratio Arm A / Arm B
results.setup: NCOG life table (47 monthly rows) fit as independent binomials y_k ~ Bi(n_k, h_k), logit(h)=X alpha with spline knots at month 11, fit separately per arm; hazards peak at month 5 then decline.
results.quote: in a ratio of about 2.5 to 1 after the ﬁrst year

results.claim: EM on the bivariate normal with 20 of 40 x2 values missing converges to correlation 0.823, but slowly (about 20 iterations; step 1 gives 0.162).
results.setup: Missing x2 initialised at 0; E step replaces x2 by its conditional expectation (9.43); M step uses standard complete-data MLEs (9.42). Final values: mu2 1.064, sigma2 .769, rho .823; mu1 1.86 and sigma1 1.08 fixed from step 1.

results.note: Column order in the extraction is mu1, mu2, sigma1, sigma2, rho inferred from the caption and footnote 11; headers are garbled.

limits: Life table estimates can go badly wrong if hazard rates change over time (footnote 3).
The log-rank test ignores the lost-to-followup counts l, which could carry information if early losses were concentrated in one arm; conditioning costs some power, usually small.
Proportional hazards inference depends on the model (9.32) being correct; efficiency of partial likelihood is claimed only under that assumption.
Formulas assume no ties among survival times for convenience.
Methods cover right-censoring and left-truncation; left- and right-censoring need more elaborate treatment. Censoring is distinct from truncation.
EM convergence can be sluggish (mu2 and rho in Table 9.8).
Greenwood's formula under censoring relies on successive conditional independence rather than independence of hazard estimates.
practices: Use Kaplan-Meier curves, with Greenwood confidence limits, to compare censored survival graphically rather than a t-test or Wilcoxon test (Sec 9.2).
Compare arms with the log-rank test, summing (y_i - E_i) across periods, not Z_i or Z_i^2, to gain power against a consistent hazard ordering (Sec 9.3, tactic 4).
Compare hazard rates, not only survival curves, because they are more informative (Sec 9.2, Fig 9.2).
Use Cox partial likelihood to regress censored survival on covariates without specifying the baseline hazard (Sec 9.4).
Standardize continuous covariates to mean 0 and sd 1 so coefficients are comparable (Table 9.7).
Use a parametric spline on the logit of hazards when more accuracy than the nonparametric life table is wanted (Sec 9.2).

terms.definition: h_i = f_i / S_i = Pr{X = i | X >= i}, the probability of dying at age i given survival past age i-1; continuous h(t) = f(t)/S(t).
S(t) = Pr{T >= t}, equal to exp(-integral of h(x) dx from 0 to t).
Survival times known only to exceed the reported value, marked with a + sign; patients lost to followup or still alive at study end.
Life table estimate with time unit going to zero: S(j) = product over k<=j of ((n-k)/(n-k+1))^d(k).
Z = sum (y_i - E_i) / (sum V_i)^(1/2) over per-period 2x2 tables with hypergeometric mean E and variance V; also Mantel-Haenszel or Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel; depends only on ranks.
h_i(t) = h0(t) exp(c_i' beta), equivalently S_i(t) = S0(t)^theta_i; semiparametric because h0 is unspecified.
L(beta) = product over observed deaths j of exp(c_ij' beta) / sum_{k in R_j} exp(c_k' beta), treated as an ordinary likelihood.
R_j = {i : t_i >= T(j)}, individuals still under observation just before the j-th death time.
Iterative missing-data method: E step fills in missing values by conditional expectation under the current estimate; M step applies standard complete-data maximum likelihood.
Generating artificial complete data from f_theta_hat(o)(u|o) does not change the MLE; MLE is self-consistent.
Redistributing each censored case's probability mass to the right per the Kaplan-Meier curve leaves the curve unchanged; the KM estimate is the nonparametric MLE of a survival function.

lineage.note: Origin of the log-rank test; Cox (1958) gives an early analysis.
Partial likelihood as justification for proportional hazards.
Codified and named the EM algorithm.
Verified Kaplan-Meier self-consistency and coined the name.
Shows partial likelihood is highly efficient for estimating beta.
Justifies replacing unconditional with conditional variances and asymptotic normality of log-rank Z.
